caseStudies.title: Focus Vault
caseStudies.cardSummary: Designed a browser productivity extension for deep work: blocking distractions, enforcing session timers, and applying Calm Technology principles to reduce interruption without friction.
caseStudies.summary: A Chrome extension that flips the focus blocker model: instead of blocking what distracts you, it defines what you need. Full product arc from discovery interviews through PRD, metrics, roadmap, and Calm Technology principles.

content.text: When a user is trying to focus in a particular browser tab, the presence of other open tabs creates a constant source of distraction. The average user has 17 tabs open at any given time. Productivity communities consistently identify tab-switching as a primary focus killer.
Discovery method: Personal experience as a proxy user, validated through five structured user interviews. Core discipline: ask about the past, never the future.

A Chrome extension allowing users to initiate a timed focus session capped at 90 minutes. Once a session begins, the browser locks to a pre-defined group of approved tabs. If a user attempts to exit early, a 15-second countdown prompts confirmation. The goal is pause, not punishment.

caseStudies.title: Spotify: Discover Music
caseStudies.cardSummary: A strategic recommendation to solve genuine music discovery for the niche listener segment using a two-layer data architecture: behavioral history plus a community music intelligence layer trained on genre-specific listener communities.
caseStudies.summary: A strategic recommendation to solve genuine music discovery for the niche listener segment. Spotify's existing infrastructure creates a structural ceiling: the more specific a user's taste, the less useful features become over time. Discover Music proposes a natural language discovery mode powered by a two-layer data architecture including a community music intelligence layer.

content.text: Spotify's recommendation engine is a feedback loop anchored to listening history, structurally favoring popular content. The algorithm shifted further toward familiarity in 2025 Autoplay, the AI DJ, and Song Radio now recycle tracks users already know.

Only 27% of users agree that streaming services help them discover music outside familiar territory. 42% actively disagree representing hundreds of millions of users whose primary discovery need is structurally unmet.

Discover Music: a new tile on the Spotify home screen where users describe the music they want in natural language. Spotify generates a playlist from the full catalogue not just listening history powered by a community music intelligence layer built from genre-specific listener communities.

items: Text input: written descriptions anchor output to specific intent, unlike the AI DJ's conversational persona
Full track playback: serves the job of finding music to save and return to
History-off mode: listening history ignored entirely the DJ cannot offer this

content.text: At 293 million premium subscribers at ~$11/month, a 1% improvement in retention represents over $38 million in annualised revenue. Discover Music targets the cohort at highest churn risk.

caseStudies.title: Goodreads: Rediscovering Discovery
caseStudies.cardSummary: A product improvement recommendation for Goodreads: four interlocking components to fix broken discovery and untrustworthy reviews, feeding directly into Amazon's $28B book revenue.
caseStudies.summary: Amazon bought Goodreads in 2013 and abandoned it. 180 million members, only 3.4% actively engaged, and no meaningful product updates in over a decade. The problem is not a lack of resources. Amazon already owns the Kindle data, the purchase ecosystem, and the community. A better Goodreads is not a product investment. It is a revenue protection play for a $28 billion book business.

content.text: Goodreads has two structural failures: users cannot find books that match their taste, and they cannot trust the reviews they see. A five-star rating system with no nuance, recommendations based on popularity rather than taste, review bombing with no moderation, and a Kindle integration gap between two Amazon products that barely talk to each other.
180 million registered members. Only 3.4% are actively engaged. StoryGraph, a direct competitor, saw 25,000 sign-ups in a single day from users who had given up on Goodreads.
Four interlocking components targeting both problems simultaneously. The first two fix discovery. The second two fix trust.

items: Redesigned Onboarding: a 5-question preference quiz at signup, genre-weighted highest, with a lighter flow for returning readers
Weighted Recommendation Engine: genre as the primary filter, taste signals ranking results within the filtered pool, learning continuously without new forms
Kindle Integration: already-read books excluded automatically, completion pace as engagement signal, abandoned books creating negative signals
Trustworthy Review System: multi-dimensional ratings, mandatory comments below 3 stars, timing-based spike detection, and Verified Reader badges weighted higher in public ratings

content.text: Amazon owns the data that could fix Goodreads. Kindle knows which books a user finished, how fast, and which were abandoned. No competitor can build this. Amazon already has it.

caseStudies.title: Notion: Guided Mode
caseStudies.cardSummary: A feature recommendation to solve Notion's structural activation problem: 100M users, only 4M paying. Guided Mode is a reactive AI assistant that helps middle users find their footing without changing the power user experience at all.
caseStudies.summary: Notion has a retention problem its headline numbers obscure. 100M users, 4M paying, a ~4% conversion rate against a 5-8% best-in-class benchmark. The gap is not a pricing problem. It is an activation problem. Guided Mode is a user-triggered AI assistant built as a free tier of Notion AI, designed to bring middle users to the product's value without touching the power user experience.

content.text: A significant portion of Notion's 100 million users never get past the blank canvas. They sign up, face an empty page with infinite options, and either give up or find a simpler alternative. These users are not failing because Notion is a bad product. They are failing because Notion was never designed for them.

The middle user wants a tool that is collaborative enough for group work and capable enough for personal writing, without requiring significant time to configure. This user exists in large numbers inside Notion's own user base they signed up, but they have never seen the product work for them.

Notion Guided Mode: a user-triggered AI assistant built into Notion as a free tier of Notion AI. It explains features in plain language, suggests templates based on the user's stated goal, and walks users through setup step by step. It activates only when explicitly asked. It does not surface suggestions proactively, does not modify the interface, and does not affect any user who does not engage with it.

items: User-triggered only: the guide never activates unless a user asks Notion's data never conflates guided users with successful users
Toggle on/off: power users can disable it permanently; middle users keep it on; two user types, one product surface
Free tier of Notion AI: paywalling the guide would charge users for the solution to a problem Notion created

content.text: A middle user who gets comfortable with Notion through the free guide is a much warmer conversion target for paid Notion AI than a cold user staring at a blank canvas who never experienced the product's value.

caseStudies.title: Predictive Road-Status Detection
caseStudies.cardSummary: A product spec turning Google Maps' diversion-reporting gap into a civic-infrastructure signal, detecting closures from aggregate travel-time data instead of citizen reports.
caseStudies.summary: Regular commuters know their routes well enough that they rarely open a navigation app, so the people most likely to encounter a new diversion are exactly those least likely to be generating data about it. This spec proposes a two-source detection system, passive travel-time inference plus a municipal data partnership, that infers road diversions and closures without requiring any citizen reporting, and reframes the output as a general civic-infrastructure signal product rather than a single Maps feature.

content.text: Regular commuters know their routes well enough that they rarely open a navigation app. The people most likely to encounter a new diversion are exactly those least likely to be generating data about it, a structural blind spot that costs India's top four cities an estimated $22B a year in peak-hour traffic delay.

A USDOT-backed study comparing Waze's crowdsourced incident reports against official state-agency logs found that only 4% of reports for local-road disabled vehicles ever reached a DOT log, versus ~40% on highways. The gap is largest on exactly the kind of familiar, local roads this spec targets.
Two sources covering each other's blind spot. No citizen reporting required at any point.

items: Passive inference: watches aggregate travel-time patterns over a few days to catch diversions that build up naturally. Blind spot: day one, before any history exists to compare against.
Municipal data partnership: a direct feed from traffic police on planned closures and construction, ahead of time. Blind spot: coverage, since it's only as good as the partnership.
Combined system: passive inference carries day-to-day coverage, the municipal feed closes the day-one gap for planned work.

content.text: Not every anomaly is a diversion; an accident or a broken-down truck produces the same traffic-pattern anomaly as a real diversion. The classification rule is the decay curve, not the anomaly alone: an incident drops back to baseline within a day, a diversion stays flat or gets worse past that window.

Strip out the navigation UI and this is a general "what changed on this road" signal, applicable to waterlogging, a fallen tree, or a burst pipe, none of which get reliably reported either, for the same structural reason diversions don't.

In a single event in November 2025, 57 localities across Chennai reported waterlogging and roughly 400 MTC buses, about a third of the fleet, were grounded. The reframe: not a Maps feature, but a real-time civic issue feed sold to municipal traffic and disaster-response departments as inferred-incident data, with navigation apps as just one distribution channel.
